source.title: Self-scalable Tanh (Stan): Faster Convergence and Better Generalization in Physics-informed Neural Networks
source.authors: Raghav Gnanasambandam; Bo Shen; Jihoon Chung; Xubo Yue; Zhen Kong

record.tranche_reason: Tests gradient training and claims about stationary points using PINNs and function approximation, but on regression and differential-equation tasks rather than the benchmark classification settings in the versions.
record.gate_note: Reports training-loss outcomes for the proposed Stan activation and tanh/N-LAAF comparators. Results for cited prior work are not extracted. No CIFAR or classification results are reported.
record.test_reason: The study compares activation functions in fully connected regression networks and PINNs. Its results do not test any specified version: regression loss is not CIFAR classification error; its stationary-point argument does not examine ReLU teacher-student width; and its activation-parameter initialization sweep does not test signal-preserving weight initialization or trainable depth. It cites Safran and Shamir but does not test their width-dependent finding.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Stan improves convergence and prediction on their regression and PINN examples, especially with large output magnitudes, and assert a conditional no-spurious-stationary-point theorem. Their low-loss experiments illustrate successful optimization; they do not establish the absence of spurious stationary points.
record.recipe_differences: Proposes a trainable self-scalable tanh activation for PINN and regression tasks; the listed claim versions concern other architectures, datasets, or training conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by activation function and task; the initialization of Stan's trainable parameters is also examined.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.1 reports lower training loss for Stan than tanh and N-LAAF on two unnormalized function-approximation problems. Table 1 also reports lower test MSE: 185.46 versus 1369.60 and 988.18 for the smooth function, and 23.97 versus 47.77 and 37.32 for the discontinuous function.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trainable Stan activations improve optimization and prediction on the tested regression functions.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections 4.1–4.2 report better PINN training outcomes with Stan, including approximately zero loss on the two ODE examples and recovery of thermal diffusivity, while both comparators estimate negative diffusivity. Table 2 reports the lowest test MSE and relative error for Stan on all four problems.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stan improves optimization and solution accuracy on the tested forward and inverse differential-equation problems.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3 asserts that gradient-descent limit points are not spurious stationary points under explicit initialization, differentiability, representational, regularization, and learning-rate assumptions. It does not establish a width effect in ReLU teacher-student networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated theorem assumptions, gradient descent on the regularized Stan objective has no spurious stationary-point limit points.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.2 varies the common initial value of Stan's trainable activation parameter across ten values from 0.25 to 1.15 and reports stable final training relative error on both regression functions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stan's final regression training performance is robust to the tested constant initial activation-parameter values.

record.problems: The empirical studies concern regression and PINN problems rather than classification benchmarks. Training results are mostly conveyed by figures; numerical test metrics are given for selected tasks. The theoretical result is conditional on explicit assumptions, including initialization and learning-rate conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows map to the six claim versions: the reported tasks and measures do not test the behaviors those versions name.

untested.parts: Training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and the stated size and training-recipe qualifications.
Spurious-minimum frequency in two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks and its dependence on teacher size and extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks, and residual training without normalization.
Activation-matched weight initialization, signal and gradient propagation across depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and maximum trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to initial stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature evolution, and edge-of-stability behavior.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparison with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. Empty result rows and labels are appropriate because none of the six versions is tested. The activation-initialization sensitivity result also belongs outside those versions.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification, random or corrupted labels, model size, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiments, spurious-minimum frequency, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual shortcut depth comparisons, deep tanh networks, and residual training without normalization.
Initialization comparisons for signal/gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and very deep plain networks.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature changes, and edge-of-stability behavior.
Batch normalization comparisons, training-speed/learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup without normalization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
